leaderPrimer:
At least one person at your table may be deciding whether to leave the church, and they won't say so. They've come to listen, quietly testing what the study says against a wound they carry, and these five weeks are part of how they'll decide. Lead with that in mind.

The hazard runs two ways. Defend the church too quickly, explaining away abuse cover-ups and baptized politics and preaching shaped by donors, and the wounded will rightly conclude this is one more room where the institution matters more than the injured. But let the group become a weekly grievance session with no second movement, and you'll have run an exit interview and called it a Bible study. The study refuses both: truthful about the mess and steady about the body. Holding that line in a live room is harder than it looks on the page.

Hear every wound all the way to the end before any "yes, but." Some of what gets named will be indefensible. Don't defend it. Say it was wrong, grieve it, and later, in its own time, let the study make its slow case. If anyone discloses abuse, take it seriously, follow up privately, and don't treat it as a group discussion topic. Abuse by a church leader should be reported to the authorities. The help information printed with this guide, and Find Help on this site, are there for those moments; keep them within reach.

I'm a pastor, I've failed the church in my own ways, and I'm still here. Go first in the self-examining questions and keep your answers short. And remember that your group isn't discussing the church from a distance. A handful of flawed people committed to the same room for five weeks is a church in miniature, and how you bear with one another is part of the argument. Someone is watching to see whether belonging is survivable.

faq.q: Is this study going to defend the church and tell me my problems with it aren't a big deal?
faq.a: No. It names the church's failures plainly: hypocrisy, division, covered-up abuse, the marriage of faith to political power. Session 3 calls the scandal a real scandal, and session 5 grants that the deconstruction movement has named real wounds. What the study refuses isn't your grievance but the conclusion that the answer to a flawed church is no church.

faq.q: Can I follow Jesus on my own without belonging to a church?
faq.a: The study says no, but not because there's a rule against it. The New Testament simply has no category for it. When God saves you he makes you part of a people, a body, a household, a temple of living stones, and none of those images works with one person. Paul says "you are the body of Christ and individually members of it" (1 Corinthians 12:27), and a member in his sense is a limb, which can't thrive cut off.

faq.q: If the church is full of hypocrites, why would I belong to it?
faq.a: Because a hospital full of sick people isn't an argument against hospitals. Jesus said he came for the sick, not the well (Mark 2:17). If the church is a gathering of the sick under a physician's care, finding it full of sinners is what it claims to be. The deeper scandal is a church that pretends it isn't sick. And the study is plain that we're all patients, the writer included.

faq.q: What about the church that hurt me badly? Is the study telling me to go back and commit?
faq.a: No. The call to commit and stay is for the ordinary flawed church, full of sinners who disappoint in ordinary ways. It is never a call to remain in an abusive church, under a predator or a tyrant or a community that covers up evil and won't repent. Leaving such a church is faithfulness to Christ, not a failure of loyalty. Honor the wound. Get to safety and to help. Abuse by a church leader should be reported to the authorities.

faq.q: I'm deconstructing my faith. Is this study going to attack me?
faq.a: No. It grants that deconstruction has named real wounds, and that much of its critique is fair. What it does, gently, is say where the road often ends: not in the promised freedom but in isolation, a faith taken apart into a private spirituality of one. It doesn't ask you to stop asking questions. It asks you not to mistake the rubble for freedom.

faq.q: Is church just the Sunday service and the building?
faq.a: No. The New Testament word, ekklesia, means an assembly of people called out and gathered, and it never means a building. Paul's main image is a body, not an event. Buildings and services matter, but when they become the whole of what we mean by church, we've mistaken the shell for the body inside it.

faq.q: What does it mean that the church is sent? Isn't mission for pastors and missionaries?
faq.a: Peter calls every believer part of a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). Following Lesslie Newbigin, session 4 argues that God's people gather on Sunday in order to be scattered all week, each carrying the gospel into places no pastor will ever go. The church doesn't hire missionaries to do the mission for everyone else. The whole church is sent.

faq.q: Why does the study talk about a refuge becoming a bunker?
faq.a: The church really is a refuge, a place of rest and shelter, and the study says so. But a refuge is meant to gather people so it can send them out stronger, like a base camp. When the church becomes only a refuge, it becomes a bunker that exists to defend itself. The difference is direction: a refuge gathers in order to send; a bunker gathers in order to hide.

faq.q: Why should I formally commit or become a member instead of just attending?
faq.a: Committing says publicly to a particular flawed people: I'm yours, you can count on me, I won't leave the first time you disappoint me. The study grants that membership can become an empty formality, so the paper isn't the point. The point is the difference between a guest who stays while satisfied and a family member who has bound themselves to a people for better and worse.

faq.q: What does Bonhoeffer mean that I have to give up my dream of community?
faq.a: In Life Together he wrote that the person who loves his dream of community more than the actual Christian community becomes its destroyer. Many of us love an ideal picture of fellowship and blame real people for not matching it. Bonhoeffer calls the shattering of that picture a grace, because only then can we love the forgiven sinners God actually gave us. Letting the dream go isn't settling for mediocrity; it's stepping down from the judge's bench.

faq.q: Does the study promise that if I commit, my disappointments will go away?
faq.a: No. It deliberately ends at the door of a decision rather than with a resolution, because life in the church doesn't get a tidy ending this side of heaven. The church you commit to will still disappoint you. What the study offers is a way of belonging that doesn't depend on the church earning it, patterned on how Christ loved the church before she was lovely.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Why does any of this matter to someone who isn't sure about God?
faq.a: The study tries to earn an answer by not pretending the church is better than it is. But there's a claim here worth weighing from the outside. Newbigin argued that the world reads whether the gospel is true mainly from the life of a congregation that believes it. If that's right, the most useful thing a skeptic can do is not read about the church but watch a real one over time, and ask whether the way these flawed people treat one another can be explained by anything other than what they say is true.

timeline.event: At Sinai God tells Israel, "you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6), the calling Peter later applies to the church.
Jesus tells Peter, "I will build my church" (Matthew 16:18), one of only two Gospel passages that use the word.
At Pentecost the first church is formed, devoted to the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers (Acts 2:42).
Paul writes 1 Corinthians, calling the church the body of Christ and ruling out the eye that says to the hand, "I have no need of you."
Ephesians says Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (authorship and date are debated).
1 Peter tells scattered Christians they are a royal priesthood and a holy nation (date debated).
Cyprian of Carthage writes On the Unity of the Church, arguing that no one can have God for Father who does not have the church for mother.
Augustine, against the Donatists' demand for a pure church, argues that wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest.
The Augsburg Confession describes the church as the assembly in which the gospel is purely taught and the sacraments rightly administered.
Luther's On the Councils and the Church lists the marks by which God's people can be recognized.
Bonhoeffer leads the Confessing Church seminary at Finkenwalde until the Gestapo closes it.
Bonhoeffer is hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April.
Lesslie Newbigin publishes The Gospel in a Pluralist Society, calling the congregation the hermeneutic of the gospel.
The deconstruction movement grows, largely online, naming real wounds of spiritual abuse and control.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thanks for being here. The church is one of the hardest things to talk about openly, especially in a room that's part of one, so three things before we start. First, this is a safe room. You can say "the church hurt me" here, and no one is going to rush to defend the institution against your pain. Second, this study takes the church's failures seriously, all of them, and it won't tell you your wounds are no big deal. It also won't take the easy exit of saying the answer to a flawed church is no church, and we're going to sit in that tension together. Third, I'm inside this too. I've loved the church, been hurt by it, and been the disappointment myself. Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a minute before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, into the actual church we belong to, or have left, or are circling warily, and into the real people and real wounds we carry.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop here, even though it isn't resolved, because our relationship to the church doesn't resolve on a schedule. Take this toward Christ and toward his people this week rather than carrying it alone. Try the practice, and spend some time with the reflection questions. If tonight brought up a real wound, or a real decision about where you belong, please bring it to someone you trust, and if you're not safe, use the help information printed with this guide. Let me pray for us before we go.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, agree the ground rules about safety and wounds, and walk through session 1's opening questions slowly. Say plainly that committing never means staying under abuse.
Week 2: Session 1, What the Church Actually Is, full discussion and practice.
Week 3: Session 2, Life Together, with extended time on Bonhoeffer and the death of the dream of community.
Week 4: Session 3, The Marks and the Mess, part one through the marks of a true church and the hospital image.
Week 5: Session 3 continued: the scandal of a divided and hypocritical church, with room for real wounds, and the practice.
Week 6: Session 4, Sent, Newbigin and the church gathered to be scattered, with time to name each person's actual mission field.
Week 7: Session 5, Committing to a Flawed Church, handled with care for anyone who has been abused or is deconstructing.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit the five practices and the decision each person is facing about where and how they'll belong.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, what the church is and the death of the dream of community.
Week 2: Session 3, The Marks and the Mess, with extended time on the hospital of sinners and the real scandal of the church's failures.
Week 3: Session 4, Sent, the church gathered to be scattered as a kingdom of priests.
Week 4: Session 5, Committing to a Flawed Church, with a short closing conversation on the whole study.

glossary.definition: Not a building or an event but a people: those called out by God and bound to him and to one another. The New Testament's names for it, body, household, temple, flock, all need more than one person.

The Greek word translated church. It means an assembly called out and gathered; in Greek cities it named the citizens' assembly, and in the Greek Old Testament the assembly of Israel. It never means a building in the New Testament.
Paul's central image for the church: Christ is the head and believers are its members, each depending on the whole, the way a hand depends on the arm.
The Reformation signs of a true church: the Word rightly preached, the sacraments rightly administered, and, in many confessions, discipline. They say what the church is for, not who gets kept out.

The church taking sin seriously because it loves the sinner, aiming at restoration (Matthew 18:15-17; Galatians 6:1). Not removing the flawed, since the church is made of them, but refusing to call sickness health.
An old saying, drawn from Jesus' words about coming for the sick (Mark 2:17): the church is a place of treatment for the not-yet-healed, not a museum of the already holy.
Bonhoeffer's phrase in Life Together for the ideal picture of fellowship we carry and often love more than the real people God gives. Its shattering, he says, is a grace.
The truth that every believer, not a special class, is part of a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), representing God to the places they're sent.
Newbigin's phrase for how a watching world reads whether the gospel is true: through the life of a congregation that believes it and lives by it.
A refuge shelters people in order to send them out stronger. A bunker gathers people only to defend itself and keep the world out.
Taking apart an inherited faith. It has named real wounds of abuse and control; the study takes it seriously while saying that its road often ends in isolation rather than freedom.

A binding of persons that doesn't depend on continued satisfaction and makes room for failure and forgiveness. It's the form of God's bond with his people, and the pattern for committing to a church. It never obliges anyone to stay under abuse.
The invisible church is the whole company of the redeemed, known to God. The visible church is the mixed body you can see and join, with true believers and hypocrites together until the harvest.
Peter's image for believers being built together into a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5). One stone alone isn't a house.
